claims.text: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys can possess a fine lamellar microstructure of alternating soft FCC and hard BCC/B2 phases.
A controlled sub-solvus aging treatment can induce nanoscale coherent precipitates in the target eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The aging-induced precipitates will be uniformly distributed at the lamellar phase interfaces.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can contribute to a combination of high tensile strength and ductility.
Nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent precipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations that could otherwise initiate premature cracks.
Facilitated dislocation transmission and reduced stress concentration improve tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated as-cast eutectic HEA, aging will produce a statistically significant increase in yield and tensile strength.
Relative to the untreated as-cast eutectic HEA, aging will improve uniform tensile ductility.
Strength and ductility will each improve by approximately 10–20% or more.
The as-cast baseline has minimal nanoprecipitate formation.
The intervention is effective only in eutectic HEAs whose compositions and processing conditions permit coherent precipitate formation.
Non-optimized aging can produce incoherent or overgrown precipitates that degrade ductility.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility changes depends on alloy composition, aging temperature and time, and service environment.
An as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA can retain an excellent combination of strength and ductility up to 700 degrees Celsius.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires improved ductility, but the falsification rule accepts mere non-reduction in ductility as a successful result. Thus an outcome with unchanged ductility would fail the stated prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
